 Prabowo Apologizes to Singapore, Malaysia Over Transboundary Haze
 Prisma Ardianto 
 November 16, 2026 | 4:25 am 
 SHARE 
 URL berhasil di salin.
 President Prabowo Subianto attends the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila, the Philippines, on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. (Courtesy of the Presidential Press Bureau/Muchlis Jr) 
 Manila. President Prabowo Subianto on Sunday offered an apology on behalf of the Indonesian government and people for the impact of forest and land fires on neighboring Singapore and Malaysia, pledging tougher action against companies implicated in the fires.
 Speaking at the ASEAN Summit in Manila, Prabowo reaffirmed Indonesia's commitment to preventing forest fires and said his administration would not tolerate corporate involvement in activities responsible for the recurring environmental crisis.
 The president assured regional leaders that Indonesia had made every effort to contain the fires and had taken a series of enforcement measures, including revoking corporate concessions and pursuing criminal investigations.
 “We have revoked 17 corporate concessions, while 26 companies are currently under investigation. Eleven companies have been charged, and another 23 are on the list of companies to be charged. In total, 104 companies are under investigation by our police,” Prabowo said.
 ADVERTISEMENT
 Indonesia has been battling forest and land fires for nearly four months, with smoke from the blazes spreading across national borders and affecting communities in Malaysia and Singapore.
 Read More:
 Indonesia Says Malaysia, Singapore ‘Welcome’ Eased Haze 
 Prabowo said the government had mobilized 71,000 personnel to combat the fires, at a considerable human and operational cost.
 “We have deployed 71,000 forest firefighters. We lost 16 people, and many more were injured while fighting the fires. We also lost two helicopters,” the president said.
 Shifting Focus to Fire Prevention 
Prabowo stressed that Indonesia needed to fundamentally change its approach to forest and land fires, moving beyond firefighting and disaster mitigation toward systematic prevention.
 The government is preparing to establish a new agency and introduce programs aimed at strengthening the country's capacity to prevent future fires, he said.
 Transboundary haze has long been a source of concern in Southeast Asia, particularly during prolonged dry seasons when forest and peatland fires in Indonesia can send smoke across neighboring countries.
 ASEAN adopted its Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution in 2002, establishing a regional framework for preventing and monitoring forest and land fires and mitigating their cross-border impact. Indonesia ratified the agreement in 2014.
